p.src: Lately Yojirō had been going around the university selling tickets for the Literary Arts Association. After two or three days, he appeared to have sold one to nearly everyone he knew. Yojirō then decided to accost people he did not know. He usually caught them in the corridors. Once he did, he would not readily let them go. One way or another, he managed to make them buy. Sometimes the bell rang in the middle of his negotiations and his quarry escaped. Yojirō called this “the hour being against him.” At other times, the other fellow merely smiled, and nothing definite could be settled however long they talked. Yojirō called this “the man being against him.” Once he caught a professor coming out of the lavatory. Wiping his hands with a handkerchief, the professor said, “Not just now,” and hurried into the library. After that, he never came out at all. Yojirō called this—nothing at all. Watching the professor’s retreating figure, he informed Sanshirō that the man must have intestinal catarrh. When asked how many tickets he had been entrusted to sell, Yojirō said he had been told to sell as many as he could. When asked whether there was some danger of selling so many that the audience would not fit into the theater, he said there was a little. Pressed that this would cause trouble after the tickets were sold, he remained unruffled and said, “Oh, it’ll be fine. Some people buy merely out of obligation, some will be kept away by mishaps, and a few cases of intestinal catarrh are bound to turn up too.” Watching Yojirō sell tickets, one saw that he naturally took the money at once from anyone who offered it in exchange, but to students who did not, he simply handed over the ticket. To the timid Sanshirō, the number he handed out as he went seemed enough to cause alarm. When asked whether all the money came in afterward as expected, his answer was that of course it did not. He said he did it this way because, on the whole, it was more profitable to sell a great many carelessly than a few with scrupulous precision.

p.src: “These are students of Tokyo Imperial University, you know.” “Students or not, plenty of them must be as easygoing about money as you are.” “Oh, the Literary Arts Association surely won’t make a fuss over anyone who fails to pay in good faith. However many tickets are sold, it is perfectly clear that in the end they will merely become the Association’s debts.” To make sure, Sanshirō asked whether this was Yojirō’s opinion or the Association’s. Yojirō gave the conveniently worded answer that it was of course his own opinion—and the Association’s as well. After listening to Yojirō’s arguments, one began to feel that anyone who did not attend the performance must be a perfect fool. Yojirō expounded until he had made one feel exactly that foolish. It was not entirely clear whether he did this to sell tickets, because he genuinely believed in the performance, or merely to work himself into high spirits, then raise the other person’s spirits, then the performance’s, and thereby make the whole atmosphere of society as lively as possible; and because these motives could not be clearly distinguished, the other person, despite feeling like a fool, was not greatly influenced by Yojirō. First, Yojirō spoke of the tremendous effort being devoted to the members’ rehearsals. If one took him at his word, most of the members seemed likely to be worn out by their rehearsals before the day of the performance. Then he spoke of the scenery. The scenery was said to be so extraordinary that every promising young painter in Tokyo appeared to have been recruited and each allowed to display his talents to the full. Next he spoke of the costumes. From head to toe, the costumes had been fashioned in strict accordance with historical precedent. Next he spoke of the plays. They were all newly written, and every one of them was interesting. And there was any amount more besides. Yojirō said he had sent complimentary tickets to Professor Hirota and Mr. Haraguchi.

p.src: On the evening of the victory celebration, Yojirō came to Sanshirō's lodgings. He was utterly unlike the man he had been that afternoon. He sat stiffly beside the brazier, complaining again and again of the cold. But his expression suggested that the cold was not all that troubled him. At first he leaned almost over the brazier, holding out his hands to the heat, but before long he tucked them inside his kimono. Hoping to brighten Yojirō's face, Sanshirō moved the lamp on the desk from one end to the other. But Yojirō merely let his chin sag, while the lamplight darkly illuminated nothing but his large, close-cropped head. He showed no sign of perking up. When Sanshirō asked whether something was wrong, he raised his head and looked at the lamp. “Doesn't this house have electricity yet?” he asked, though the question had nothing whatever to do with his expression. “Not yet. I hear they mean to install it before long. Lamps are no good—they're too dim,” Sanshirō was saying, when Yojirō, apparently forgetting the lamp altogether, suddenly began, “Listen, Ogawa, something terrible has happened.” Sanshirō first asked him what had happened. Yojirō pulled a badly crumpled newspaper from inside his kimono. There were two sheets folded together. He peeled one away, refolded it, and thrust it toward Sanshirō, telling him to read there. He held his fingertip on the passage. Sanshirō brought his eyes close to the lamp. The headline read, “The University's Pure Literature Department.” It said that the university's foreign-literature department had hitherto been staffed by Westerners, with those in charge entrusting all instruction to foreign teachers; but, prompted by the advance of the times and the wishes of many students, the university had now finally decided to make lectures by a Japanese scholar a required part of the curriculum as well. A search for a suitable candidate had therefore been under way for some time; a certain gentleman had at last been selected, and an announcement was expected shortly. The article concluded that the gentleman was an exceptionally gifted man who had recently received orders to study abroad and was therefore eminently suited to the post. “So it wasn't Professor Hirota after all,” Sanshirō said, turning to Yojirō.

p.src: “Is this certain?” Sanshirō asked again. “I don't know.” Yojirō cocked his head. “I thought it was almost certain we'd succeed. We've bungled it. Though I had heard that this fellow had been doing a great deal of lobbying,” he added. “But this is still only rumor, isn't it? We won't know until the official announcement is actually made.” “No, if that were all, it wouldn't matter, of course. It has nothing to do with Professor Hirota. But—” Yojirō refolded the remaining newspaper, held his fingertip on the headline, and placed it beneath Sanshirō's eyes. This newspaper carried much the same story. That part alone could hardly have made any fresh impression on him, but what followed startled Sanshirō. It portrayed Professor Hirota as a man of shocking moral turpitude. Though he was a mediocrity who had taught languages for ten years without ever becoming known to the public, the moment he heard that the university intended to appoint a Japanese lecturer in foreign literature, he began furtively lobbying for the post and circulating laudatory accounts of himself among the students. Moreover, he had induced one of his disciples to write an essay entitled “The Great Darkness” for a minor magazine. The essay had appeared under the pseudonym “Mukago,” but it was known, the article claimed, to have been written by one Ogawa Sanshirō, a student in the College of Letters who frequented Hirota's house. And there at last was Sanshirō's own name. Sanshirō looked at Yojirō with a peculiar expression. Yojirō had already been watching Sanshirō's face. For a while, neither of them spoke. At length Sanshirō said, “This is awkward.” He felt somewhat resentful toward Yojirō. Yojirō paid little attention to that. “What do you make of this?” he asked. “What do I make of it?” “They must have printed a letter to the editor just as it was sent in. There is no possibility that the newspaper investigated it themselves.”

p.src: Any number of letters like this come in, set in six-point type, for the literary review column. Six-point type is practically a mass of wickedness. When you look into them carefully, many turn out to be lies. Some contain the most blatant lies. And why do they do anything so foolish, you ask? It seems they are all motivated by questions of personal interest. So when I was in charge of the six-point submissions, I threw nearly all the malicious ones into the wastebasket. This article is exactly the same sort of thing. “It is the result of a campaign against us.” “Why did they print my name instead of yours, I wonder?” Yojirō merely said, “Yes, indeed.” After a while, he began, “I suppose it must be because—” “You are a regular student and I am a special student,” he explained. But to Sanshirō this was no explanation at all. Sanshirō remained as troubled as ever.

p.src: “The trouble is, I should never have used a paltry pen name like Mukago; I should have boldly signed it Sasaki Yojirō. “The truth is, there is not another soul besides Sasaki Yojirō who could have written that essay.” Yojirō was serious. Perhaps he was actually distressed that Sanshirō had usurped his authorship of “The Great Darkness.” Sanshirō found the whole thing absurd. “Have you spoken to the professor?” he asked. “Ah, that is precisely the point. “It does not matter whether you or I am taken for the author of ‘The Great Darkness,’ but now that the professor’s character is involved, I cannot keep silent. “Knowing him, I might ordinarily say, ‘I know nothing about it; there must be some mistake. An essay called “The Great Darkness” did appear in a magazine, but it was anonymous and written by an admirer of yours, so please do not worry.’ He would simply say, ‘Is that so?’ and the matter would be over—but I cannot do that now. “Whatever happens, I must make my responsibility clear. “When things have gone well, it feels good to pretend not to know; but when they have gone wrong, keeping silent is unbearably unpleasant. “Above all, after starting the whole affair myself and putting such a good man in this painful position, I cannot simply stand by and watch without a care. “Leaving aside difficult questions of right and wrong, I simply feel too sorry for him, too full of pity to bear it.” For the first time, Sanshirō thought Yojirō an admirable fellow. “Do you suppose the professor has read the newspaper?” “It was not in the paper delivered to his house. “That is why I did not know about it either. “But the professor goes to the university and reads all sorts of newspapers there. “Even if he has not seen it himself, someone will surely tell him.” “Then he already knows.” “Of course he does.” “Has he said anything to you?” “No.

It would be better if he at least had a child. He really leads an austere, detached life.” Yojirō folded his arms. “And whenever I try to cheer him up by going to a little trouble, this is what comes of it. You should go and see the professor too.” “I can hardly go merely to see him. I bear some responsibility myself, so I’m going to apologize.” “You have no need to apologize.” “Then I’ll go explain myself.” With that, Yojirō left. After getting into bed, Sanshirō tossed and turned again and again. He felt that he slept more easily back home in the country. The false article—Professor Hirota—Mineko—the impressive man who had come for Mineko and taken her away—there were all sorts of agitations. From midnight onward, he slept soundly. Getting up at his usual hour was exceedingly difficult. At the washstand he met another student from the Faculty of Letters. They knew each other by sight, and no more. From the way the man greeted him with a polite “Good morning,” Sanshirō inferred that he had apparently read the article in question. The other man, of course, avoided the subject. Sanshirō made no attempt to explain himself either. While breathing in the aroma of hot soup, he received another letter from his mother back home. As usual, it looked likely to be long. Changing out of his Western clothes was too much trouble, so he put on hakama over them, slipped the letter inside his coat, and went out. Outside, a light frost gleamed. Just inside the gate stood a large pine tree. Its branches spread like a gigantic umbrella, screening the entrance hall. p.src: Peering briefly through the gate, Sanshirō repeated the word “Hydriotaphia” twice under his breath. Of all the foreign words Sanshirō had learned, this was one of the longest and also one of the most difficult. He still did not know what it meant. He intended to ask Professor Hirota about it. When he had once asked Yojirō, Yojirō had said it was probably something like “data fabula.” But to Sanshirō, there was an enormous difference between the two. “Data fabula” sounded like something one ought to dance to. “Hydriotaphia” took time even to memorize. Repeating it twice naturally slowed one’s pace. It sounded as though the ancients had coined it expressly for Professor Hirota’s use. Once at school, he felt as though all eyes were fixed on him as the author of “The Great Darkness.” He tried to go outside, but it was unexpectedly cold, so he stayed in the corridor. Then, between lectures, he took his mother’s letter from inside his coat and read it. It contained an order that he come home for the winter holidays, just as in the days when he had been in Kumamoto. In fact, something like this had happened while he was in Kumamoto. Just as school was about to break up—or perhaps even before it had—a telegram arrived telling him to come home. Convinced that his mother must be ill, he rushed home in alarm, only to find her delighted, as if to say how fortunate it was that nothing had happened to him. When he asked why, she said that because she had waited and waited and he still had not returned, she had consulted the Inari deity; the oracle declared that he had already left Kumamoto, and she had therefore been terribly worried that something might have happened to him on the way. Remembering that episode, Sanshirō wondered whether she would consult the oracle again this time. But the letter said nothing about the Inari deity.

Once at school, he felt as though all eyes were fixed on him as the author of “The Great Darkness.”
He tried to go outside, but it was unexpectedly cold, so he stayed in the corridor.
Then, between lectures, he took his mother’s letter from inside his coat and read it.
It contained an order that he come home for the winter holidays, just as in the days when he had been in Kumamoto.
In fact, something like this had happened while he was in Kumamoto.
Just as school was about to break up—or perhaps even before it had—a telegram arrived telling him to come home.
Convinced that his mother must be ill, he rushed home in alarm, only to find her delighted, as if to say how fortunate it was that nothing had happened to him.

When he asked why, she said that because she had waited and waited and he still had not returned, she had consulted the Inari deity; the oracle declared that he had already left Kumamoto, and she had therefore been terribly worried that something might have happened to him on the way.
Remembering that episode, Sanshirō wondered whether she would consult the oracle again this time.
But the letter said nothing about the Inari deity.

p.src: Sanshirō sat down before the long brazier. The iron kettle was singing away. The old woman tactfully withdrew to the maid's room. Sanshirō sat cross-legged, warming his hands over the iron kettle as he waited for the professor to wake. The professor was fast asleep. The quiet put Sanshirō pleasantly at ease. He tried tapping the iron kettle with his fingernail. He poured hot water into a teacup, blew on it, and drank. The professor lay asleep with his face turned away. He seemed to have had his hair cut two or three days earlier, for it was extremely short. The edges of his beard showed darkly. His nose, too, pointed away. His nostrils breathed with a soft whistle. He was sleeping peacefully. Meaning to return it, Sanshirō took out the Hydriotaphia he had brought and began to read. He read bits and pieces here and there. It was exceedingly difficult to understand. It said something about throwing flowers into graves. It said that the Romans “affect” roses. He did not really know what it meant, but supposed it probably translated as “favor.” It said that the Greeks use Amaranth. That was not clear either. Still, it had to be the name of a flower. A little farther on, he lost the meaning altogether. He took his eyes from the page and looked at the professor. He was still asleep. He wondered why the professor had lent him such a difficult book. Then he wondered why this difficult book held his interest even though he could not understand it. In the end, he concluded that Professor Hirota was, after all, Hydriotaphia itself. Just then Professor Hirota abruptly sat up. He raised only his head and looked at Sanshirō. “When did you get here?” he asked. Sanshirō urged him to sleep a little longer. In truth, he had not been bored. “No, I'll get up,” said the professor, and rose. Then, as usual, he began puffing philosophical smoke.

p.src: “Thank you. I'm returning your book.” “Ah. —Did you read it?” “I did, but I couldn't make much sense of it. To begin with, I don't understand the title.” “Hydriotaphia.” “What does it mean?” “I don't know what it means either. At any rate, it sounds Greek.” Sanshirō lost the courage to ask any further. The professor gave a yawn. “Ah, I was sleepy. I had a fine sleep. And I had an interesting dream.” The professor said it had been a dream about a woman. Sanshirō thought he was going to tell him about it, but instead the professor asked whether he would like to go to the bathhouse. The two of them set out with towels dangling from their hands. After their bath, they stepped onto the apparatus set on the wooden floor and measured their height. Professor Hirota was five shaku six sun tall. Sanshirō was only five shaku four sun five bu. “You may still grow,” Professor Hirota told Sanshirō. “No, it's no use. I've been this height for three years,” Sanshirō replied. “Is that so?” said the professor. Sanshirō thought the professor must regard him very much as a child. When they returned home, the professor said that if Sanshirō had nothing else to do, he was welcome to stay and talk; then he opened the study door and went in first. Sanshirō followed him in, since in any case he had a duty to settle that other matter. “It seems Sasaki isn't back yet.” “He said he would be late today and gave notice. p.src: “Did you see that article in the newspaper?” “Yes, I did.” “You knew nothing about it until it appeared in print?” “No.” “You must have been surprised.” “Surprised—well, I cannot say I was not surprised at all. But I take everything in this world to be much the same, so I cannot be as honestly surprised as a young man would be.” “It must be troublesome for you.” “I cannot say it is no trouble at all. But among men of my age, who have lived in the world as long as I have, not everyone who reads that article will immediately take it for fact; so again, I cannot feel as honestly aggrieved as a young man would. Yojirō knows someone on the newspaper staff, so he talks all sorts of nonsense about measures to repair the damage: asking the man to publish the truth, tracking down the source of that letter and punishing whoever sent it, or issuing a thorough rebuttal in his own magazine. If he is going to all that trouble, it would have been infinitely better not to stir up needless trouble in the first place.” “We truly did it for your sake, Professor. We meant no harm.” “I should hope you did not do it out of malice. To begin with, if people campaigning on my behalf adopt whatever methods and set whatever course they please without even asking what I want, is that not the same as making a mockery of my very existence from the outset? You cannot imagine how much easier it is to preserve one’s dignity by simply having one’s existence ignored.” Sanshirō had no choice but to remain silent. “And then you went and wrote that worthless thing called ‘The Great Darkness.’ —The newspaper says you wrote it, but I hear Sasaki was actually the author.” “That is right.” “Sasaki confessed last night. You are the one who has truly been put in an awkward position. No one but Sasaki could have written such a foolish piece. I read it myself.

p.src: It has neither substance nor dignity; it is nothing but a Salvation Army drum. One can only suppose it was written to provoke ill feeling in its readers. From beginning to end, it is constructed entirely out of contrivance. Anyone with common sense would conclude that it was written with some ulterior purpose. No wonder they say I had one of my disciples write it. When I read it, I thought the newspaper article quite justified indeed.” With that, Professor Hirota brought the discussion to an end. As usual, he blew smoke through his nostrils. Yojirō claimed that he could tell the professor’s mood by the way this smoke emerged. When it gushed out thick and straight, the professor had reached the supreme heights of philosophy; when it loosened and dispersed gently, his spirits were tranquil, though there was a chance he might begin teasing someone. When the smoke lingered beneath his nose as though reluctant to leave his mustache, he was entering meditation. Or else he was seized by poetic inspiration. Most terrifying of all was a whirl at the very mouth of the nostril. When a whirl appeared, one was in for a severe scolding. Since this was Yojirō’s story, Sanshirō naturally placed no faith in it. But under the circumstances, he watched the shape of the smoke with particular care. Yet none of the distinct varieties Yojirō had described appeared at all. Instead, what did emerge possessed nearly all those characteristics at once.

p.src: Since Sanshirō remained deferentially withdrawn no matter how long he waited, the professor began speaking again. “Let us say no more about what is already done. Sasaki apologized for everything last night, so by now he is probably cheerful again, darting about as usual. There is no point in reproaching his misconduct behind his back when the man himself is calmly going about selling tickets and the like. Let us talk about something more interesting instead.” “Yes.” “While I was napping a little while ago, I had an interesting dream. You see, it was a rather novel-like tale in which I suddenly met again, in a dream, a girl whom I had seen only once in my life; but it is more enjoyable to hear than a newspaper story.” “Yes. What sort of girl was she?” “A pretty girl of twelve or thirteen. She had a mole on her face.” Hearing that she was twelve or thirteen, Sanshirō felt a little disappointed. “When did you meet her?” “About twenty years ago.” Sanshirō was surprised again. “How did you know it was that same girl?” “It was a dream. Because it was a dream, I simply knew. And because it was a dream, there was nothing wrong with its being strange. I seemed to be walking through a vast forest. I was wearing that faded summer suit of mine, you know, and that old hat. —Yes, and at the time I seemed to be pondering something difficult. All the laws of the universe are unchanging, yet everything in the universe governed by those laws must change. If so, those laws must exist apart from things themselves. —It seems foolish once one is awake, but because I was dreaming, I was earnestly thinking such thoughts as I passed beneath the trees, when suddenly I came upon the girl. We did not happen to cross paths. She was standing perfectly still before me. When I looked at her, her face was exactly as it had been long ago. She was dressed exactly as she had been long ago. Even her hair was as it had been long ago. And of course the mole was still there.

p.src: In short, she was still the same twelve- or thirteen-year-old girl I had seen twenty years before, unchanged in the slightest. When I told her that she had not changed at all, she replied that I had grown very old. Then I asked how she had managed to remain so unchanged, and she said that she stayed as she was because she liked best the year of this face, the month of these clothes, and the day of this hair. When I asked when that had been, she said it was twenty years ago, when she met me. When I wondered aloud why, then, I had grown so old, the girl explained that it was because I had always wished to move on from what I was then toward something ever more beautiful. Then I said to her, ‘You are a picture,’ and she said to me, ‘You are a poem.’” “What happened after that?” Sanshirō asked.

p.src: “And then you came along,” he said. “When you say you saw her twenty years ago, that wasn’t a dream but something that really happened?” “What makes it interesting is that it really did happen.” “Where did you see her?” Smoke once again streamed from the professor’s nostrils. A great many of us went out carrying rifles, having been told that we were to attend the minister’s funeral. I thought we were going to the cemetery, but we were not. The gymnastics instructor marched us inside Takebashi and lined us up along the roadside. We remained standing there and were to see the minister’s coffin on its way. It was called seeing him off, but in truth we were little more than spectators. It was a cold day; I remember it even now. Standing motionless, my feet began to ache inside my shoes. The fellow beside me kept looking at my nose and saying how red it was. Presently the procession arrived. It was an exceedingly long one, as I recall. One quiet carriage and rickshaw after another passed before my cold-stricken eyes. Among them was the little girl I just told you about. Even when I try now to recall the scene as it was, everything is hazy and refuses to take clear shape. Only that girl remains in my memory. p.src: “That is why I what?” “Is that why you have never married?” The professor burst out laughing. “I am not such a romantic creature as that. I am made of far more prosaic stuff than you.” “But if that girl had come to you, you would have married her, wouldn’t you?” “Well…” he said after considering it a moment. “I suppose I would have.” Sanshirō looked almost as though he felt sorry for him. The professor then began to speak again. “To say that this forced me to remain single would be the same as saying that the girl had crippled me. But some people are born with a kind of infirmity that makes marriage impossible. And there are others whose various circumstances make marriage difficult.” “Are there really so many circumstances in the world that stand in the way of marriage?” Through the smoke, the professor gazed steadily at Sanshirō. “Hamlet probably had no wish to marry. There may have been only one Hamlet, but there are many people like him.” “What kind of person, for example?” “For example…” the professor said, and fell silent. Smoke poured out incessantly. “Suppose, for example, there is a certain man. Suppose his father died young and he grew up relying solely on his mother. Then his mother falls ill, and at the very moment when she is about to breathe her last, she tells him that after her death he must place himself in the care of a certain person. She names someone the child has never met and knows nothing about. When he asks why, his mother gives no answer. When he presses her, she says in a faint voice that this certain person is in fact his real father. —It is only a story, of course, but suppose there were a child with such a mother.
